text: {"score":4,"justification":"The summary is accurate and well grounded. Its numbers match the card (27.1% vs 1.7%, z 4.29, adjusted score 26.46, 84% low complexity, 4 of 8 documented 99215s below billed vs peers 9%, 2 of 18 data-without-tests). The overpayment figures ($11,492, CI $5,486-$17,497) come from the estimate tool output, so they are grounded despite the number check flag. Cited claims fit their sentences: three documented-below-billed examples and three low-complexity 99215s. Next steps are concrete, and the summary includes a coder-review caveat. Weaknesses are a few overstatements and some redundancy.","problems":["Rationale says 'The charts back up the claims pattern', which is stronger than the evidence supports. Only 8 documented 99215s exist, and the 'documented below billed' flag is a moderate MDM vs high, not proof of error.","'The high share is mostly on healthy patients' is loose wording; the 0-1 condition patients are not necessarily healthy. It also repeats the 84% figure stated earlier.","Headline says 'Random sample of 30 charts: 7 below billed level', but 7 spans 99214s and 99215s. The mix is not clearly explained, and the 4 of 8 figure is a small denominator without a stated caveat.","The low-complexity examples are all 1-condition patients, so they do not show the more striking zero-condition cases. Heart failure and atrial fibrillation also arguably carry real complexity, making them weaker illustrations.","The summary does not flag missing items, such as the small documented sample (2.3% of claims) or that 4 of the 5 high-complexity 99215 claims are not discussed.","The overpayment estimate is presented with a CI but is extrapolated from a tiny sample. The caution is brief, and the standard 'reason to review, not a finding' sentence from the draft was dropped."]}
